# The Strange Comfort of Impermanence

I've been thinking lately about how we spend so much energy fighting against the nature of things. Not in some grand philosophical sense, though there's that too—I mean in the small, daily ways we resist what's actually happening in favor of what we wish were happening instead.

Last week, I watched a man at a coffee shop spend forty-five minutes trying to get the perfect photograph of his cappuccino. He'd take a shot, examine it on his phone, adjust the cup slightly, move it toward the light, then away from it, try a different angle. The cappuccino was getting cold. I'm certain it was getting cold because I could see the foam flattening, the latte art that had been precise and geometric becoming something softer and less defined. At some point, he seemed to accept this and took a drink, but his expression suggested he was disappointed—not with the taste, necessarily, but with the fact that the perfect moment had passed.

I recognized myself in him immediately.

There's something peculiar about living in an age of perfect preservation. My parents have a handful of photographs from their childhood, grainy things that captured moments but were ultimately irreplaceable. That limitation created a kind of acceptance. You took the photo, you hoped it turned out, and then you moved on. But now we can take hundreds of photos in a single afternoon. We can edit them, filter them, crop out the parts that don't serve the narrative we're constructing. We can take them again and again until we get it right. And somehow, this abundance of control has made us feel more out of control than ever, more anxious about capturing the "right" version of our lives.

The cappuccino foam was going to dissolve. That was its nature. It was literally designed to dissolve, to be temporary. And maybe—this is what I keep coming back to—maybe that was exactly what made it beautiful.

I think about impermanence a lot. Partly because I read too much Japanese philosophy, partly because I'm at an age where I'm suddenly noticing that things I took to be permanent fixtures are starting to disappear. My grandfather's bookshelf is being emptied. My childhood home is being renovated by its new owners. A restaurant I went to every other week for seven years closed last month without any warning. Friends have moved to new cities and the old rhythm of seeing them regularly just... stopped.

When you're younger, this kind of loss feels catastrophic. It feels like the world is ending. But there's something interesting that happens if you sit with it long enough: you start to see that the ending of one thing is always the condition for the beginning of another. The cappuccino's foam has to dissolve for you to actually drink the coffee. Your childhood home has to be left behind for you to have an adult life. That restaurant had to close to make room for whatever comes next.

This doesn't make loss painless. I'm not trying to write some motivational piece where I convince you that everything is fine because the universe recycles. Loss is real, and grief is appropriate, and sometimes things end that you wish had continued. But I think there's a difference between accepting that grief and believing that impermanence is a design flaw in the universe that we need to overcome.

We seem determined to overcome it, though. Look at how much of our technology and culture is bent toward preservation and permanence. We digitize everything. We archive. We back up. We have storage units full of things we haven't looked at in decades because we can't bear to throw them away. We post our lives on social media as if creating a permanent record of our days might somehow protect us against time. We talk about legacy and immortality and the fact that our digital presence might outlive our physical bodies.

Is that comforting or terrifying? I can't decide.

What strikes me is that in pursuing permanence, we seem to have made ourselves less present. If you're constantly documenting something, are you actually experiencing it? If you're trying to preserve a moment perfectly, are you allowing the moment to simply be what it is? There's a paradox in all this—we want to hold onto life, so we turn it into data, into records, into something static and safe. And in doing so, we miss the life that's actually happening, the one that's always moving, always changing, always dissolving like foam on cooling coffee.

I read somewhere that the Japanese have a concept called *mono no aware*—the pathos of things. The idea that there's a deep beauty and poignancy in transience itself. The cherry blossoms in spring are beautiful partly because they bloom briefly and then fall. If they bloomed year-round, they'd lose something essential. Their meaning is bound up with their impermanence. That's not a defect. That's the point.

I wonder what we'd appreciate differently if we really internalized this. Would we experience ordinary moments more vividly if we accepted that we couldn't preserve them? Would we be kinder to people if we acknowledged that our time with them is limited and unpredictable? Would we complain less about aging if we stopped seeing it as something to resist and started seeing it as the condition that makes life mean anything at all?

There's a Japanese practice called *shinrin-yoku*—forest bathing. It's not about exercise or accomplishing anything. You just walk through a forest slowly, taking it in. No photographs (or at least not as the primary goal), no hiking to a destination, just being present with the changing light through the trees, the smell of soil, the sound of things living and dying. People report that it's profoundly calming. I think part of why is that you can't preserve a forest bath. You can't capture it. You can only have it, and then it's gone, and then you have something else.

I've started trying to do this more. Not literally in forests (though I do that too), but in regular life. I'll sit at dinner with someone I care about and instead of pulling out my phone to take a photo, I'll just... sit there. I'll notice the way the light catches their face when they laugh. I'll notice details I would never have seen through a camera lens. And when the evening ends, I won't have documentation of it. I'll just have the memory, which is fragmented and imperfect and will probably fade over time. And somehow, knowing that makes it feel more real, not less.

It's hard to do this consistently. The impulse to preserve is strong, especially when you love something or someone. The thought of losing it terrifies us. So we reach for whatever tools we have to hold onto it—photographs, journals, social media posts, repeated conversations about the past. Sometimes these things help. Mostly, I think they're a way of trying to negotiate with time itself, trying to convince it not to take what we love.

Time doesn't negotiate.

But here's what I've noticed: the things I remember most vividly aren't the ones I tried hardest to preserve. They're often random moments I didn't try to capture at all. A conversation in a car on a cloudy afternoon. The way my friend laughed at a joke that probably wasn't even that funny. The smell of a specific season in a specific place. These memories feel more real to me than any photograph, and I think it's because I was actually present for them. I wasn't observing them from the remove of a recording device. I was in them, living them, while they were still alive and changing.

Maybe the reason we're so anxious is that we're not actually living many of our lives. We're curating them, editing them, trying to turn them into something more permanent and presentable than the raw, messy, temporary thing that actually is.

I think about this especially around milestones. We treat them like they should be permanently crystallized—the perfect wedding day, the perfect graduation, the perfect vacation. And we work so hard to make them perfect that we miss the actual experience of them. Perfection is static. Life is not. Life is a cappuccino where the foam dissolves whether you wanted it to or not. It's a moment that's already over the second it begins.

What if we stopped treating that as a problem?

What if we accepted that everything we love will eventually be lost, and that that's not a tragedy but a feature? That it's what makes love feel urgent and necessary? That it's what transforms an ordinary moment—coffee with a friend, a conversation with your child, a day at the beach—into something that matters?

I'm not saying we shouldn't preserve anything. Memory is valuable. Art is valuable. Records are valuable. But maybe we should preserve things differently than we're doing it now. Maybe we should preserve them less obsessively, more lightly. Maybe we should document some moments while allowing others to fade, as a way of practicing the acceptance we'll need anyway.

Because everything fades. Your childhood home will be renovated. The restaurant you love will close. Your favorite songs will start to sound dated. The friends you see every day will move away. Your own face will change in the mirror. The small aches will become bigger ones. People you love will die. You will die.

And you know what? That's okay. It's not okay like "everything works out and there's a happy ending." It's okay like "this is what life is, and the only way to feel less alien in it is to accept it rather than resist it."

The funny thing is, I think accepting impermanence might be what actually lets us enjoy things. Not constantly reaching for the camera, not performing our lives, not trying to make everything permanent and perfect. Just being in it. Just living it. Just knowing it will end and appreciating it anyway.

That cappuccino will be cold eventually. But right now, at this moment, it's warm. Right now, it's exactly what it is—temporary, specific, unrepeatable. The man at the coffee shop could have spent forty-five minutes taking pictures, or he could have spent forty-five minutes actually tasting it, noticing it, being present with it.

I wonder which choice he would have regretted less.

I wonder which choice any of us will regret less, when we're at the end, looking back at all the moments we didn't quite allow ourselves to have because we were too busy trying to preserve them.
